articles.title: Adjusted For Inflation, Net Tuition Costs Are Declining At Public Universities
articles.summary: Adjusted for inflation, tuition and fees at public colleges and universities are cheaper now than they were a decade ago. according to the College Board’s la...
articles.body:
Adjusted for inflation, tuition and fees at public colleges and universities are cheaper now than they were a decade ago. according to the College Board's Trends in College Pricing and Student Aid 2026 report released last week.

Between academic years 2016-17 and 2026-27, average inflation-adjusted tuition and fees remained unchanged for students attending private nonprofit colleges and universities, while they declined by 8% for public four-year in-state students, and decreased by 12% for public two-year in-district students. Those are significant turnarounds compared to increases of 20% or more in each of those sectors during the previous two decades.

After adjusting for inflation, 42 states saw declines in their average in-district tuition and fees at public two-year colleges, and 41 states saw declines in their average in-state tuition and fees at public four-year institutions in the last five years.

According to the report, the average published tuition and fees for AY 2026-27 were:

$12,290 for in-state students at public 4-year colleges, up $350, or 2.9%, over the previous year;

$32,730 for out-of-state students at public 4-year colleges, up $1,110, or 3.5%;

$4,210 for in-district students at public two-year colleges, up $100, or 2.4%; and

$46,350 at private nonprofit 4-year colleges, up $1,640, or 3.7%.

These annual increases, shown above, are before adjusting for inflation.

Published "sticker" tuition prices attract the lion's share of press coverage, frequently sensationalized by headlines of tuition costs closing in on or crossing the $100,000 mark, but they convey a false impression about the true costs of college tuition. For that number, we need to consider "net tuition," which is the cost that students actually pay after receiving institutional and other financial aid grants. Those figures write a different narrative. Inflation-adjusted net tuition costs have fallen on average over the past decade:

After adjusting for inflation, the average net tuition and fees paid by first-time, full-time in-state students at public four-year institutions peaked in 2012-13 at $4,600 (in 2026 dollars) and declined to an estimated $1,920 in 2026-27;

The average net tuition and fees (in 2026-27 dollars) paid by first-time full-time students enrolled in private, nonprofit four-year institutions stayed roughly the same at about $20,000 (in 2026 dollars) between 2006-07 and 2019-20 before dropping to an estimated $17,280 in 2026-27.

On average, first-time, full-time, in-district students attending public two- year colleges have received enough grant aid to cover their tuition and fees since academic year 2009-10.

articles.title: Trump’s $1.5 Trillion Defense Budget to Be Blocked by Democrats
articles.summary: Republicans’ midterm defeat is crushing any remaining hopes that Congress would approve President Donald Trump’s unprecedented $1.5 trillion defense budget r...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Republicans' midterm defeat is crushing any remaining hopes that Congress would approve President Donald Trump's unprecedented $1.5 trillion defense budget request amid an unpopular war in the Middle East.

Democrats, who won solid majorities of both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, were already largely opposed to the 44% increase from the previous fiscal year and are now signaling they will block any efforts to push it forward.

At the same time, Republican lawmakers returning to the lame-duck session before the new Congress is seated in January may not be able to muster the support or political will to ram through the massive defense spending package, especially amid the Pentagon's unpopular war against Iran that cost many of them their jobs.

"We must push for the development of a more realistic and sustainable approach to our national security — one that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or one paid for with draconian cuts to critical domestic programs," Representative Adam Smith of Washington, the incoming chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, said in a statement after the election.

The Democratic resistance risks imperiling some of Trump's splashiest defense ambitions, including the Golden Dome missile shield and his Trump-class battleship plan, and bodes poorly for defense contractors — some of which also face the prospect of congressional scrutiny over alleged conflicts of interest with the Trump administration.

Shares of major contractors, including Lockheed Martin Corp. and Northrop Grumman Corp., fell this week as the midterm results eroded expectations of a ramp-up in US military spending.

Lawmakers returning to Washington on Monday are going to have to grapple with the annual defense policy bill and a spending plan for fiscal year 2027 — which began on Oct. 1 under stopgap funding that runs out on Dec. 11. Both those measures are now in limbo.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth justified Trump's steep fiscal 2027 budget request by arguing the funds would kickstart badly needed defense modernization efforts as autonomous systems change modern warfare.

But the sheer size of the increase — combined with domestic spending cuts, the growing costs of the Iran war and expensive projects like the Trump-class battleships — grated on lawmakers, including Republicans. And newly emboldened Democrats are likely to be far more motivated to kill off these massive defense spending plans than Republicans are to defend them in the lame-duck session.

articles.title: Facebook recovery scams use fake FBI profiles
articles.summary: Facebook ads promising to recover stolen funds are targeting scam victims again, and Meta confirmed removing flagged accounts after investigation.
articles.body: You've already lost money to a scam. You're frustrated and probably wondering whether you'll ever see that money again. Then, while scrolling through Facebook, an advertisement appears promising to recover your stolen funds. Suddenly, there's a little hope. Maybe someone out there can actually help. Unfortunately, that moment of hope is exactly what scammers are trying to exploit. One of our loyal CyberGuy followers, Patrick K, recently tipped us off to suspicious fraud recovery advertisements and profiles appearing on Facebook. He shared screenshots of what he was seeing and urged us to warn others. His tip caught our attention, so we decided to dig deeper and contacted Meta about the suspicious accounts and advertisements. After reviewing the examples we provided, Meta confirmed to CyberGuy that it removed the flagged accounts and ads for violating its impersonation policies. The screenshots Patrick shared are especially concerning. One promotes stolen-asset recovery services. Another uses FBI-related imagery and claims to help people navigate the Internet Crime Complaint Center, better known as IC3. Together, they show how convincing these offers can appear. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. WHY IDENTITY THEFT COMES BACK FOR THE SAME PEOPLE Facebook recovery ads promise to get your money back The first screenshot Patrick shared shows a Facebook advertisement displayed under the name Adam Molina. The promotional image features a smiling man in a business suit against a purple background. The graphic bears the name "DARKTRACER" and asks whether you've lost assets or funds to scammers. Below that message, the ad promotes services like recovering stolen assets and retrieving hacked cryptocurrency wallets. At the bottom, there's a Facebook Messenger button inviting people to send a message. That's what concerns me. Someone who just lost thousands of dollars could see this advertisement and believe they've finally found a solution. After all, it looks like a company offering specialized assistance. And because it appears as a paid Facebook advertisement, some people may assume the advertiser has been thoroughly vetted. Fake FBI investigator profiles create another trap The second screenshot Patrick sent us is even more troubling. It shows a Facebook page displaying the title "Director of Fraud Investigations" and the name Grace K. The cover image features the White House, the FBI's J. Edgar Hoover Building and cryptocurrency graphics. It also displays references to IC3 and the U.S. Department of Justice. The page description claims to help fraud victims navigate the IC3 reporting process. It even suggests that people who lost more than $4,000 may qualify for federal review. That claim appears on the page, but we found no support for such a dollar threshold in the FBI's published guidance. It's a convincing presentation for someone desperately searching for help. The American flags and official-looking graphics create the impression that a federal agency may be involved. But here's what you need to know. The FBI says IC3 has no official social media presence. It never investigates crimes or recovers stolen money through Facebook Messenger or Telegram. That means any Facebook page claiming to represent IC3 should immediately raise suspicion, regardless of how official it looks. Meta's subsequent removal of the flagged accounts and advertisements reinforces those concerns. Meta removes Facebook recovery scam accounts after CyberGuy inquiry After CyberGuy shared Patrick's screenshots with Meta, the company investigated and confirmed that it removed the flagged accounts and advertisements for violating its impersonation policies. Meta also provided broader details about its efforts to combat these schemes. According to the company, it removed more than 179 million accounts, Pages and Groups for misrepresenting identity during the first half of 2026. Most were removed before anyone reported them. Since 2025, Meta says it has also removed more than 17.3 million Facebook and Instagram accounts linked to criminal scam centers. This problem isn't new to Meta. The company previously worked with cybersecurity researchers at Graphika to identify fraudulent websites impersonating the FBI's IC3 complaint center. The scammers promised to help victims recover stolen money, including cryptocurrency. Meta says it blocked the fraudulent websites and removed accounts connected to those operations. However, the examples Patrick discovered show how these impersonation schemes continue to reach Facebook users. FBI warns about fake IC3 recovery investigators On July 20, 2026, the FBI issued an updated public warning about scammers impersonating IC3 investigators. According to the agency, criminals create fraudulent social media profiles that appear connected to the FBI. They then approach people who have already reported losing money to online scams. In one documented scheme, a victim realizes they've been defrauded and threatens to report the crime to the FBI. Later, someone pretending to be an FBI agent contacts the victim through Facebook Messenger. The conversation may move to Telegram, where the impersonator provides a link supposedly connected to the victim's IC3 complaint. That link may contain malicious code or collect additional financial information. Either way, the victim faces another potential loss. The FBI also warns about AI-generated videos impersonating federal officials. Some of these videos direct victims to fraudulent websites designed to resemble the real IC3 complaint center. Once there, visitors may be asked to submit personal information under the impression they're dealing with federal investigators. And this type of impersonation extends well beyond Facebook. In a separate September 17, 2026, warning, the FBI reported nearly 61,000 complaints involving law enforcement or government impersonation scams between January 2025 and July 2026. Reported losses exceeded $1.6 billion. Those figures cover a broad range of government impersonation schemes, not Facebook recovery scams specifically. However, they show how costly impersonating official authorities has become. SCAMMERS ARE COMING FOR YOUR MONEY. HERE’S THE ONE THING YOU MUST NEVER DO Why scammers target people who already lost money There's a particularly cruel element to recovery fraud. The criminals approach people who may already be dealing with serious financial hardship. Some have lost retirement savings, while others have been tricked into sending cryptocurrency to someone they trusted. When an offer arrives promising to recover those funds, it's understandable why someone might want to believe it. In August 2026, the Federal Trade Commission warned that recovery scammers sometimes purchase lists of people who previously lost money to fraud. They use those details to make their offers appear credible. For example, someone may contact you claiming they've located your stolen funds. They might even know approximately how much you lost. That information can make the person sound legitimate, especially when they claim to represent a government agency or law firm. Eventually, the supposed recovery agent introduces a fee. They might call it a processing charge or claim the payment will release your recovered funds. But after you pay, the promised refund never arrives. In some cases, the scammer also collects enough personal information to attempt identity theft. We've previously covered the scripts criminals use in cryptocurrency scams, including fake recovery services that demand additional cryptocurrency payments. How to spot Facebook recovery scams before losing more money A convincing advertisement or official-looking Facebook profile can fool someone who's searching for answers. Fortunately, there are warning signs you can look for before responding. Here's how to protect yourself. 1. Be suspicious of guaranteed recovery promises Anyone claiming they can definitely retrieve stolen cryptocurrency or recover all your lost money deserves close scrutiny. Recovery depends on the circumstances, and no legitimate service can guarantee success. Be especially cautious when someone promises fast results. 2. Never pay an unexpected upfront recovery fee The FTC warns that scammers often demand processing fees before supposedly releasing recovered funds. These payments may be described as taxes or administrative charges. However, the FBI says IC3 never charges victims to recover stolen money. 3. Check claims of government involvement If someone on Facebook claims to work for IC3, don't engage. The FBI says IC3 has no official social media presence. Instead, type IC3.gov directly into your browser to verify information or submit a complaint. 4. Watch for conversations moving to other apps Scammers may begin contacting you through Facebook Messenger before asking to continue on Telegram. The FBI specifically identified this behavior in IC3 impersonation cases. Be cautious when an unexpected contact pressures you to switch platforms. 5. Protect your financial information Never share banking passwords or cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases with someone advertising recovery services. Also, don't install remote-access software at the request of an unexpected contact. Doing so could give scammers access to your accounts or device. 6. Research recovery companies independently Search for the company's name alongside terms such as "scam" or "complaint." Look for independently verifiable business information and a legitimate track record. Keep in mind that scammers can create fake testimonials and misleading websites to appear trustworthy. THE BEST DEFENSE AGAINST HIGH-TECH AI SCAMS IS LOW-TECH SKEPTICISM, EXPERT WARNS 7. Use strong antivirus software Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious websites, phishing links and harmful downloads associated with recovery scams. Choose protection with real-time threat detection and web security features. Keep it updated to help defend against emerging threats. However, antivirus software cannot prevent every scam, especially if you're tricked into sending money yourself. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com 8. Consider a personal data removal service Scammers may use information from data broker websites to identify potential targets and make fraudulent recovery offers more convincing. A reputable data removal service can help remove your personal information from covered broker sites. This reduces some of the information criminals can easily find about you, although it cannot eliminate every exposure. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com 9. Report suspicious Facebook advertisements Select the three-dot menu in the upper-right corner of the advertisement and choose Report ad. Then follow the prompts. For suspicious profiles or pages, use Facebook's reporting options to flag possible impersonation or fraud. 10. Invest in identity theft protection If scammers obtain your personal information, they may attempt to use it for additional fraud. An identity theft protection service can monitor for certain signs of suspicious activity and alert you to potential misuse. Depending on the plan, it may also provide identity restoration assistance if your information gets compromised. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com 11. Save evidence before blocking the account Take screenshots of the advertisement or suspicious profile before blocking it. Also, preserve the page URL and any messages you received. These details may help Facebook and law enforcement investigate the activity. What to do if you already contacted a recovery scammer If you've exchanged messages with someone offering to recover stolen money, stop communicating until you've independently verified who you're dealing with. And if you've already sent money, act quickly. Here's what to do next. Remember, legitimate recovery options may exist through financial institutions or law enforcement investigations. Always contact these organizations directly using their official websites or verified phone numbers rather than information provided by someone who approached you online. Kurt's key takeaways I have to give Patrick credit for bringing these suspicious Facebook ads to our attention. After we followed up with Meta, the company investigated and removed the accounts and ads we flagged. That's a positive outcome, and I appreciate Meta taking action. Still, the bigger problem remains. Scammers continue targeting people who have already lost money, often using convincing government branding to gain their trust. Meanwhile, if you've lost money, don't let anyone pressure you into paying more to recover it. Contact your bank or law enforcement directly, and report suspicious ads whenever you see them. Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com Sign up for my FREE CyberGuy Newsletter Copyright 2026 CyberGuy.com. All rights reserved.

articles.title: Democrats plot to choke off Iran war — with some GOP help
articles.summary: Democrats, on the wings of the big midterm wave, are looking to grind President Trump’s war with Iran to a halt once they retake the majority next year. Senate Democrats say they have some Republican support to end the conflict, which has dragged on for more than eight months, and have threatened to use the…
articles.body:
Democrats, on the wings of the big midterm wave , are looking to grind President Trump’s war with Iran to a halt once they retake the majority next year.

Senate Democrats say they have some Republican support to end the conflict, which has dragged on for more than eight months, and have threatened to use the “power of the purse” to deprive the Pentagon of funds needed to wage the war.

Both Trump and Vice President Vance pointed to the Iran war as the main culprit for why Republicans experienced an electoral wipeout, with Democrats taking the majority in the House, Senate, governors’ mansions and statehouses.

“We are going to end the war. We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said at a press conference Wednesday.

Four Republican senators — Thom Tillis (N.C.), Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), and Rand Paul (Ky.) — previously backed Democrats on a resolution to direct the commander in chief to withdraw U.S. service members from hostilities against Iran, barring formal congressional authorization for use of military force.

Congress is staring down a Dec. 11 timeline to fund the government or suffer a shutdown, less than a month before the majorities in both chambers switch. It’s unclear whether Republicans will attempt to pass one final reconciliation bill before losing control, which could include emergency Iran war funding.

Candidates on both sides of the aisle criticized the Iran war during their campaigns, as it became less and less popular. The conflict has cost at least $47 billion , while causing energy prices to skyrocket. Trump had long promised to keep the U.S. out of foreign wars.

Some Democrats, including at least one with 2028 aspirations , said the House caucus should demand an end to Iran war funding as part of any agreement to keep the government funded, even temporarily.

“Support a continuing resolution prohibiting the financing of any combat activities of the U.S. military in Iran. End the Iran war like we did for Vietnam,” Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, wrote on social media Wednesday.

Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.), a senior member on the House Appropriations Committee, wrote on social media Friday that “we can’t wait until the next Congress to end the war with Iran – it must end NOW!”

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said this week he will introduce a joint resolution to end Iran on the first day of the next Congress.

“And Democrats will use hearings, legislation, oversight and the power of the purse to push the administration toward a durable, diplomatic solution,” Meeks said in a statement to The Hill. “We will keep fighting to end Trump’s failed war of choice, as we focus on addressing the needs of the American people.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is slated to become House Speaker in January, said in a “Dear Colleague” letter that one the caucus’s priorities will be to stop the “ reckless war of choice ” in Iran.

The White House in June requested $87.6 billion in supplemental funding, which includes $67 billion in Pentagon funding. The package has not gone far in Congress with increased Democratic opposition.

The typically bipartisan National Defense Authorization Act is on shaky ground this year amid partisan infighting. Democrats think the policy bill’s top-line number should be shaved off hundreds of billions of dollars, and they are demanding guardrails around the U.S. war with Iran.

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Saturday during Crooked Media’s “Crooked Con” event in Washington, D.C., that Democrats should halt funding for White House operations to make the president end the conflict.

“We control that. So if he can’t find a way out of this, we can put pressure on him,” Kelly said in reference to Trump. Hours later, Sen. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), who is on the Senate Intelligence Committee, endorsed Kelly’s pitch .

Rep. Nikki Budzinski (D-Ill.), who is expected to be the next chair of the New Democrat Coalition, said the Democrats’ leverage to end the Iran war rests in the funding process. But she also wants answers from the Pentagon about what victory looks like.

“I do think that it’s through the Defense budget and the appropriations process. It is the power of the purse. I think we know that this administration put out a ridiculous, eye-popping amount to Congress to fund this war. There’s going to be no appetite for that. And so, I think that that is going to be, probably, the most important tool that we’re going to have in our toolbox to hold them accountable,” Budzinski said in a phone interview with The Hill.

“But I also am eager, beyond just the appropriations process, to have them come before Congress to explain what does success — they still have not articulated what success looks like,” the Illinois Democrat said.

Some top House Republicans agree about the lack of strategy over the war, which has emptied out the U.S. military magazines of top-tier weapons systems and left U.S. bases in the Middle East severely damaged by Iranian attacks.

Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), who chairs the powerful House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, declined on Friday to say whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should be impeached or otherwise removed from office.

“But I can tell you with a high level of confidence that … there’s a lot of questions about Hegseth,” Comer said Friday during his appearance on NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcast partner.

“We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one’s happy about Iran, and I think the Republican voters are more upset about what’s going on in Iran than the Democrat voters,” Comer said.

House Democrats, who have long called for Hegseth’s removal , said the oversight will not stop there. They are also encouraging their GOP colleagues to pass a bill that would prohibit the use of additional funds for the war without congressional approval.

“And every Republican who suddenly found the courage to oppose the war come election season better put their money where their mouth is and vote to end the war and pass my bill to prevent Trump from spending a single dollar more on it,” Rep. Pat Ryan (D-N.Y.), another House Armed Services Committee member and former Army intelligence officer, said in a statement to The Hill.

articles.title: Ex-RFK Jr adviser requests records on Wiles’s health policy influence
articles.summary: Calley Means, a former top adviser to Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., requested records on former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles’s health policy influence be preserved following allegations he made that she led the Trump administration to consistently bow to corporate interests on health policy. “In light of…
articles.body:
Calley Means, a former top adviser to Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., requested records on former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles’s health policy influence be preserved following allegations he made that she led the Trump administration to consistently bow to corporate interests on health policy.

“In light of suggestions that Susie Wiles and James Blair may pursue legal action over my Joe Rogan interview, I am publicly requesting that she, Ballard Partners, Continental Strategy, and other relevant parties immediately preserve all potentially relevant records and communications,” he wrote on social media Sunday.

Means began his lengthy list asking for Wiles’s communications regarding the sugar industry’s impact on federal nutrition as well as her discussions with GOP pollster Tony Fabrizio, food industry representatives and White House officials about “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) initiatives, school nutrition standards and the proposed federal definition of ultra-processed foods.

He also listed drafts, internal correspondence, meeting notes and communications involving health officials, such as Kennedy, Walker Barrett and Heidi Overton.

The former health adviser concluded his list by requesting records from Continental Strategy — the lobbying firm Wiles’s daughter works for — be preserved.

Means, a Kennedy ally who helped build the MAHA movement, resigned from the administration two weeks ago after clashing with the White House and becoming frustrated over the lack of progress on key MAHA priorities.

He made headlines recently for accusing Wiles of ensuring special interests were making donations to the administration and the GOP to have a monetary advantage in the midterm elections.

Means claimed in an interview with podcaster Joe Rogan that Wiles once told him directly, “I need the money from the sugar people to win the midterms.”

During her tenure as a lobbyist before joining the Trump administration, Means says Wiles took money from the highest-paying clients, including from the pharmaceutical and pesticide industries, as well as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

In another interview with CBS News on Sunday, Means said he believed staffers around President Trump were giving him “severe poor advice” and treating the president “like a baby.”

images.caption: Calley Means, senior adviser to Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., speaks during an event to celebrate “improving the nation’s food supply and advancing the Make America Healthy Again agenda” at the HHS Department in Washington, D.C., on Aug. 10, 2026.

articles.title: Nvidia investigates reports of CEO’s relationship with alleged Chinese spy
articles.summary: Nvidia’s board of directors announced it would be opening an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, following reports alleging he had an intimate relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe was spying for China. “The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has…
articles.body:
Nvidia’s board of directors announced it would be opening an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, following reports alleging he had an intimate relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe was spying for China.

“The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the board wrote in a statement . “A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation.”

The board continued that it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets” were compromised by Huang’s relationship with accused Chinese spy and Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.

“The Board’s inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” it concluded. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”

The accusations stemmed from a Thursday New York Times report that claimed American spy agencies last year discovered Alice Huang illegally smuggled advanced AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with Jensen Huang.

While Nvidia and Huang denied the initial report, the CEO reportedly acknowledged on Sunday that he was “unfaithful” to his wife.

“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote, according to a Sunday report from Bloomberg , citing a memo released to the company.

Another report from the Times also found Secretary of State Marco Rubio allegedly oversaw the drafting of the 2025 memo that was sent out regarding Jensen Huang and Alice Huang’s relationship, citing multiple people briefed on the matter.

The Nvidia CEO has already been called to appear this month by a group of GOP lawmakers who chair the House Select Committee on China, House Foreign Affairs Committee and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.

They requested Huang appear in a joint, closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 to address concerns regarding Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with … Alice Huang.”

images.caption: FILE – Jensen Huang, president and CEO of Nvidia, waits for a groundbreaking ceremony for an expansion of Coherent’s manufacturing facility to begin on June 16, 2026, in Sherman, Texas. (AP Photo/Jeffrey McWhorter, File)
